entry.title: BW/4HANA vs Datasphere: how do you debug a missing delta record
entry.content:
How are you troubleshooting data issues in SAP Datasphere without an aDSO-style change log?
In SAP BW/4HANA, the aDSO change log is one of our most-used troubleshooting tools. When a report shows wrong numbers or a delta hasn't loaded properly, we go straight to the change log and can see:

🔹 Which request brought in a record
🔹 The before image and after image of every change
🔹 Exactly when a value changed and what it was before
🔹 Where the gaps are, by comparing requests against the source

In SAP Datasphere, a local table with Delta Capture only keeps the latest version of each record (Change_Type / Change_Date). The internal _Delta table isn't meant for external access, so there's no built-in way to see the old value or trace a change back to a specific load.
For those running Datasphere in production (especially with Replication Flows from S/4HANA):

1️⃣ How do you investigate a missing or wrong delta record today?
2️⃣ Have you built your own change history (append-only history table, SCD Type 2, snapshots)? What worked and what didn't at large volumes?
3️⃣ How do you reconcile Datasphere against the source to spot delta gaps?

entry.title: Stored Procedures, Task Chains, and the Reusability Problem in SAP Datasphere
entry.content:
This is not a question about AI or the latest viral trend. It's about a real-life, day-to-day problem.

When you're managing more than 200 data sources and need to orchestrate a large number of loads and objects, efficiency and reusability are not nice-to-haves, they're essential.

In our case, we need to execute a common process every time one of those 200 tables is loaded. The initial idea was to add a single Stored Procedure to each Task Chain. Unfortunately, while Stored Procedures are not blocking in SAP HANA, SAP Datasphere block them, causing the chains to fail.

The alternative of creating 200 different Stored Procedures that all execute exactly the same logic, simply to work around this Datasphere limitation, doesn't seem like a reasonable solution.

Any ideas?

How is a fundamental and widely used pattern such as code reuse supposed to be implemented in Datasphere?
 
Thanks in advance.

entry.title: Why do SAC Model and Datasphere Analytic Model use different function libraries?
entry.content:
When creating calculated measures, I notice that some functions are available in SAP Analytics Cloud but not in SAP Datasphere Analytic Models, while other functions are available in Datasphere but not in SAC.

What is the architectural reason for maintaining different calculation engines and function sets between the two products? Are there plans to align these function libraries in the future so calculations can be more easily migrated between Datasphere and SAC?

For example:

Example 1: 

In SAC, functions such as SUBSTRING() are available in calculated measures.
In Datasphere Analytic Models, equivalent string manipulation functions may be different or unavailable.

This means the same business logic often needs to be rewritten when moving calculations between the two platforms.

Example 2: 

Datasphere provides conversion functions such as TO_DATE() for converting strings into date data types, while SAC's calculated measure engine does not expose the same function.

entry.title: RAW → Harmonization → Reporting: Where should Business Logic live?
entry.content:
A common approach is:
RAW → HARMONIZATION → REPORTING → SAC

On paper, this separation looks straightforward. But in real implementation projects, the boundaries between these layers can become less obvious.

One question I’ve been thinking about while working with SAP Datasphere: Where should business logic actually live in Raw, Harmonization, or Reporting?

For example:
COGS should be calculated from specific GL accounts, with sign inversion and certain account mappings applied.

Would you typically implement that logic in the HARMONIZATION layer, so it becomes reusable across multiple reports?

Or would you keep harmonization closer to the source data and implement the business rule in the REPORTING/Analytical Model layer, where it is directly tied to the reporting requirement?

I'm particularly interested in real project experience here.

Have you encountered cases where putting business logic in the wrong layer caused problems later, such as duplicated logic, inconsistent KPIs, performance issues, or having to redesign the model close to go-live?

Are there any Datasphere-specific limitations or best practices that influence where you place this logic?

Would love to hear how others approach this in actual implementations.

Thanks.

entry.title: Cawa to Datasphere job scheduling
entry.content:
Hi all,

We want to schedule SAP Datasphere task chains from CA Workload Automation (CAWA). I haven't found a step-by-step guide for this combination.

Our requirement

Three task chains: Sales (source: S/4HANA), Delivery (source: Oracle), and Billing (source: S/4HANA).

Run order: Sales → Delivery → Billing. Each starts only if the previous one succeeds.

Sales and Delivery run daily. Billing runs only on Fridays and at month-end. If month-end falls on a weekend, it runs the preceding Friday.

My understanding so far

A CAWA agent on a server runs a script on a schedule.

The script uses the Datasphere CLI (@sap/datasphere-cli) to run the task chain and checks its status.

The script returns an exit code (0 for success, non-zero for failure) that CAWA uses for dependencies and alerts.

A Datasphere admin creates an OAuth client for the CLI login.

My questions

Is this the recommended approach, or is there a better way (for example the REST API)?

What are the exact CLI commands to run a task chain and read its final status in a script?

Is there a reliable way to get the final status of a task chain run, rather than just whether it was triggered?

Has anyone done this with CAWA (DE or AE edition)? Any pitfalls with OAuth setup, token expiry, or network access?

Thank you

entry.title: Is DP Agent Required for Connections from SAP Datasphere to External Data Sources?
entry.content:
We would like to clarify when DP Agent is required for connecting SAP Datasphere to external data sources.

Currently, we are testing a connection from SAP Datasphere to a PostgreSQL database hosted in a cloud environment (Azure in our case).

The current configuration is as follows:

SAP Datasphere → DP Agent → External Data Source (PostgreSQL on Azure)

Steps Performed

Allowlist configuration on the external system side
The public IP address of the DP Agent has been added to the allowlist on the destination side.

Connection configuration in SAP Datasphere
A connection to the external PostgreSQL database was created with the following settings:

Host: Public IP address of the external system
Database: PostgreSQL
Port: 5432
Authentication: Database username and password provided by the external system

JDBC driver configuration on the DP Agent
The required JDBC driver was placed in the designated location on the DP Agent, and the driver was loaded successfully.

Connection test
When testing the connection, the TCP connection from the DP Agent to the external system times out.

We are currently checking internally whether outbound TCP/5432 communication from the DP Agent to the external system is allowed.

However, since the external data source in this case is hosted in a cloud environment rather than on-premises, we would also like to confirm whether using the DP Agent is the appropriate architecture in the first place.

Questions
1. When SAP Datasphere connects to an external data source, is DP Agent required regardless of whether the data source is on-premises or in the cloud?
2. For a cloud-hosted data source such as PostgreSQL on Azure, is it possible for SAP Datasphere to connect directly without using DP Agent?
3. If the requirement for DP Agent depends on the connection type or data source, under what conditions is DP Agent required?

entry.title: Creating SQLScript Table Function views - the hard way
entry.content:
SAP Datasphere consultant has to create a SQL Scripting View (Table Function) with dozens of output fields, you can almost see their expression change. I have yet to meet someone who genuinely enjoys that task.

The reason is simple. SAP Datasphere is generally unable to derive the output structure of the generated function automatically (while this is certainly not a trivial capability to implement, it is also the kind of functionality one would reasonably expect from an enterprise-grade data platform), and as a result, the consultant is often forced to define the output structure manually by creating every field one by one, specifying data type, length, and other attributes individually. Repeat that process dozens of times, and what should be a simple development task quickly becomes a tedious exercise.

But Datasphere consultants are used to finding creative workarounds.

For a long time, there was a small trick that helped avoid this manual effort:

  1. Create the object as a standard SQL View.
  2. Paste the SQL statement that generates the desired output structure.
  3. Validate the view so Datasphere generates the output schema automatically.
  4. Change the view type to SQL Scripting (Table Function).
  5. Adjust the code by adding the RETURN statement and the final semicolon.

This approach could save several minutes of repetitive work and significantly improve the developer experience.

I say could because, for some time now, this workaround has stopped working reliably. In many cases it no longer works at all.

While reviewing SAP support incidents, I found SAP Note, which appears to be related to this behavior. Unfortunately, the note is quite generic. It mentions that output structure generation may fail for complex queries and even warns about the possibility of view corruption. It literally states:

"Avoid validating the SQL script prematurely during development to minimize the risk of corruption."

The recommendation leaves several open questions. What exactly constitutes validating "prematurely"? Why should pressing the Validate button at the wrong moment risk corrupting the view? And, more importantly, why is deriving the output structure still such a fragile process?

This brings us back to the original situation. Either consultants manually create the output structure field by field and lose valuable development time, or they wait until the new AI-assisted service becomes capable of handling SQL Scripting views reliably. Of course, the ideal scenario would be for the existing workaround to work consistently again, without requiring an additional paid service.

I'm curious to know how others deal with this when creating SQL Scripting (Table Function) Views. Do you define the output structure manually, or have you found a better workaround?

entry.title: How do you handle missing exchange rates without compromising financial reporting?
entry.content:
Hi everyone,

I've been thinking about a scenario that can easily become a data-quality issue in SAP Finance reporting.

Imagine we're building a Finance analytical model in SAP Datasphere. We have transaction amounts in different currencies, and we need to convert them into a common reporting currency using exchange rates from TCURR.

Now consider this scenario:

  • A transaction is posted on 15 October in USD.

  • The reporting currency is EUR.

  • The model looks for the applicable USD-to-EUR exchange rate for that date.

  • The required rate isn't available in the exchange-rate data.

What should happen next?

We could leave the converted amount empty, flag the transaction for investigation, or use the most recent available rate. Each approach has different implications for reporting accuracy.

Using the previous available rate might seem practical, but it could also produce a misleading financial figure if the business expects the rate valid for the transaction date.

I'm curious how others handle this in SAP Datasphere and S/4HANA Finance implementations.

  1. Do you fail validation when the required exchange rate is missing, or allow the model to continue with a flagged amount?

  2. If you use the previous available rate, how do you validate it and prevent an outdated rate from being used indefinitely?

  3. Where do you implement this logic: during data preparation, in the graphical view, or in the analytical model?

  4. How do you distinguish a genuinely missing rate from a rate that exists under a different exchange-rate type or quotation convention?

I'd particularly like to hear about approaches that preserve financial accuracy while keeping reporting models maintainable.

Thanks!
